chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from some of our companions from Abu al-'Ala' said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man found wealth and announced it; when a year had passed, he bought a servant from it. The seeker of the wealth came and found the girl who was bought with the dirhams was his daughter. He (peace be upon him) said: 'He is not entitled to take anything except his dirhams, and the daughter is not his; he only has his principal capital, for his daughter was owned by the people.'
From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Abdullah ibn Ja'far:

He said: I wrote to the man (peace be upon him) asking him about a man who bought a camel or a cow for sacrifice, and when he slaughtered it, he found in its belly a pouch containing dirhams or dinars or gems. Who does that belong to? He (peace be upon him) wrote: 'Announce it to the seller; if he does not know it, then the item is for you, may God grant you provision of it.'

key_terms.عَرَّفَهُ: He announced it / made it known

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on found money used to buy a slave or found inside an animal?
ai.summary: These narrations from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarify the distinction between the principal value and the appreciation or transformation of found property (*luqatah*). In the first case, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes that the owner retains only the capital spent, as the daughter was merely a commodity purchased with those funds, illustrating the principle of *istihlak* (consumption/transformation). The second ruling emphasizes the finder's duty to announce the find to the seller, ensuring transparency before claiming ownership if the seller cannot identify the hidden wealth.
